script: You want special treatment? I would love to!. Once upon the before‑time in 2015, I worked my way through nursing school as a waitress in a restaurant. I'd been grinding for months, pulling orders and learning the menu like a second language. The place didn't put up signs; it thrived on word‑of‑mouth, so everyone knew the vibe. I was the go‑to for newbies—no official title, but the trainers knew I could handle the rush and keep the crew calm. On a Wednesday, an older dude fresh out of a different location landed in my section. He was shy, nervous, and the first night of his own block. He'd heard the gossip about a demanding round table of six twenty‑somethings who'd come in a month ago. He was already sweating, asking, "They want something that's not on the menu, right?" I kept my cool. "Ask the back line; if they're good, I'll talk to the table." The cooks were fine with a wrap, so that side was clear. but here's the thing – the table's leader was a diva. Every time he brought the last item, she demanded something else. I watched him flounder, a man on a tightrope. I nodded, checked his other tables, and quietly slipped them into my own cycle. He looked like he was about to bail, and I felt like the emotional support animal he desperately needed. (I know, right?) The night ran late. The group lingered past closing; we were the last crew on our side. He came over, frantic, asking about employee discounts stacked on one ticket. "Employee?" I asked. She'd been yelling at him all meal, calling him the worst waiter, and now she wanted to stack discounts and free birthday cake for a group of "multiple birthdays." The table's boss was a trainer from another location, and she was treating the man like a dumpster. then it hit me – this wasn't just a bad shift. It was a personal attack, and my boss was the only thing standing between us and a nightmare. I told him the plan: skip the discount, get the employees' numbers, call the higher manager. He nodded, grabbed the numbers, and started a phone call while I gathered the crew. I ran to every available staff—dishwashers, busboys, even the bartender—whispering the fast rundown. The front‑end boss was a gem; he had my back and didn't want a "restaurant employee acting so cruelly." He approved the song and the cake. The table, sitting in the corner, had never seen a birthday song so loud. We lined up, sang "Happy Birthday" at full volume, and the sound bounced off the walls until everyone's ears popped. The leader's smug smirk cracked, her smile faded, and her hands covered her ears. The pain was still audible in my ears today, but the satisfaction? Unmatched. Meanwhile, my boss was on a call, reporting the incident to the general manager. The trainer got no discount, no job, and the whole thing was logged. I sat there, half‑in the chorus, half‑waiting for the phone to end. The tension was thick—like a drumbeat in a silent room—because I didn't know if she'd get fired or if we'd just keep the same old drama. The song faded, but the echo of that moment… (unfinished)
